name: Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge
blurb: Alligators, peat and blackwater in the Land of the Trembling Earth.

tip.title: Remove the alligators
tip.text: Alligators eat fish, snakes and raccoons. Set American alligator to -100% and watch what happens to bowfin, cottonmouths and raccoons.

sources.title: US Fish & Wildlife Service: Okefenokee NWR
US Fish & Wildlife Service: Fishing at Okefenokee

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Bald cypress
nodes.desc: A swamp conifer that, with swamp tupelo, dominates the forested parts of the Okefenokee. Squirrels and other seed eaters use its cones.

nodes.name: American white water lily
nodes.desc: A floating-leaved plant of the open lakes and wet prairies, which cover about 60,000 acres of the refuge.

nodes.name: Highbush blueberry
nodes.desc: A fruiting shrub of the swamp margins and islands whose berries feed birds and mammals.

nodes.name: Swamp bay
nodes.desc: A wetland evergreen tree. Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the Palamedes swallowtail.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: A common browser of shrubs and plants on the swamp islands and edges. The refuge lists it among its main mammals.

nodes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats tree seeds and nuts, including cypress, and is itself prey for hawks, owls and bobcats.

nodes.name: Palamedes swallowtail
nodes.desc: A large butterfly of southeastern swamps whose caterpillars feed on bay trees such as swamp bay.

nodes.name: Northern cardinal
nodes.desc: A seed- and fruit-eating songbird that also takes insects. It is one of the many songbirds of the refuge.

nodes.name: Eastern pondhawk
nodes.desc: A dragonfly that hunts other insects and is one of the commonly recorded dragonflies near the swamp.

nodes.name: Pig frog
nodes.desc: A big aquatic frog of lakes and wet prairies. Amphibians are called bio-indicators of environmental health by the refuge.

nodes.name: Bowfin
nodes.desc: A predatory fish that copes with the acidic, low-oxygen tannic water. The refuge names it among its common fish.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats fruit, small animals and eggs. It is also prey for alligators and bobcats.

nodes.name: Great egret
nodes.desc: A wading bird that spears fish and frogs in shallow water. Wading bird numbers shift with water levels.

nodes.name: Florida cottonmouth
nodes.desc: A venomous water snake that eats frogs, fish and other small animals around swamp water.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Scavenges carrion such as dead deer and mammals.

nodes.name: American alligator
nodes.desc: The refuge estimates about 15,000 alligators. It eats fish, snakes, birds and mammals, and its holes hold water in dry spells.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: A stealthy cat that hunts deer, squirrels, birds and rabbits across the swamp islands and edges.

nodes.name: Florida black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore of berries and animal foods. The swamp is critical habitat for the Florida black bear.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light drives plant growth, and the open tea-coloured water lets lilies and shrubs thrive.

nodes.name: Blackwater and rain
nodes.desc: The swamp depends on rainfall, and decaying plants stain the water tea-coloured. The Suwannee and St. Marys rivers drain it.

nodes.name: Drought and fire
nodes.desc: Cycles of drought and fire have shaped the wetland, shifting plants and pushing fish into deeper water.

nodes.name: Peat
nodes.desc: Peat up to about 15 feet thick covers much of the swamp floor, giving it the name Land of the Trembling Earth.

nodes.name: Fungi, bacteria & detritivores
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and dead animals and recycle nutrients into the peat.
